title: Beyond Deterrence: Evolving China-Russia Military Coordination and the U.S.-Japan Alliance
gist: A CSIS Strategic Japan report documents how the tenth China-Russia joint strategic bomber flight in December 2025 marked two qualitative escalations — it was timed to China's own Taiwan-related pressure campaign against PM Sanae Takaichi rather than shared Sino-Russian interests, and it flew more than 600 miles past the Southwest Islands on a trajectory pointing toward Tokyo. The U.S.-Japan military response escalated from two B-52s in December to an unprecedented four B-52s in February 2026, and the author argues sustained short-of-war pressure blurs the line between deterrence and compellence, requiring the alliance to plan across eight response approaches including rollback-type compellence.

themes.theme: Japan's bilateral framing of autocratic coordination

insights.claim: Japanese government documents deliberately avoid treating China, Russia and North Korea as a single bloc or new axis, instead analyzing overlapping bilateral relationships — China-Russia, Russia-North Korea, China-North Korea — separately in the Defense White Paper and Diplomatic Bluebook.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Japanese threat assessments are structured bilaterally, so headline 'axis' narratives overstate how Tokyo actually allocates defense planning and budget.
insights.quote: Japanese government documents tend not to treat China, Russia, and North Korea as a single bloc or a new axis.
insights.locator: Japan’s Threat Perception of Coordination Among China, Russia, and North Korea

insights.claim: Iran is often included in U.S. policy discussions of coordination among autocratic powers, but for Japan it remains relatively peripheral — a divergence in how the two allies define the adversary set.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Allied threat definitions differ, which complicates joint planning and signals where U.S. and Japanese defense priorities can diverge.
insights.quote: For Japan, however, Iran remains relatively peripheral.
insights.locator: In U.S. policy discussions, Iran is often included

insights.claim: An expert panel convened by Japan's Ministry of Defense has assessed that if a contingency occurs in East Asia, China, Russia and North Korea would likely coordinate.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Official Japanese planning now assumes multi-front coordination in a Taiwan or Korea contingency — a driver of larger force-structure and munitions requirements.
insights.locator: A report by an expert panel convened by Japan’s Ministry of Defense

themes.theme: China-Russia coordination as Japan's top concern

insights.claim: In Japan's 2025 Defense White Paper the term 'China-Russia' appears approximately 47 times, far exceeding references to Russia-North Korea or China-North Korea relations, which number only in the single digits.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A quantifiable ranking of Japanese threat priority — China-Russia coordination, not North Korea, is the axis driving Japanese defense policy change.
insights.quote: the term “China-Russia” appears approximately 47 times, far exceeding references to Russia-North Korea or China-North Korea relations, which number only in the single digits
insights.locator: China-Russia Military Coordination as Japan’s Primary Concern

insights.claim: Japan's Defense White Paper assesses that China and Russia seek to shape a favorable international environment by taking aligned positions on security issues including Taiwan and NATO's eastward expansion, where each is at odds with the United States.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Links the European and Asian theatres politically — positions on Taiwan and NATO are traded as a package, so escalation in one raises risk in the other.
insights.locator: The Defense White Paper also assesses

insights.claim: The development of China-Russia coordination helped prompt Japan to bring forward by one year, from 2027 to 2026, the review of its three strategic documents: the National Security Strategy, the National Defense Strategy, and the Defense Buildup Program.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: An accelerated Japanese strategy review in 2026 is a near-term catalyst for defense budget and procurement upgrades — a hard calendar item to track.
insights.locator: This concern has also been reflected at the strategic and policy level

insights.claim: China-Russia military coordination in Asia has expanded beyond senior-officer exchanges and joint exercises into operational activities including joint naval navigation and joint bomber flights, which Japan's 2025 Defense White Paper calls clearly intended as a demonstration of force against Japan and a grave concern for national security.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The shift from exercises to routine operations means pressure is now continuous rather than episodic — a permanently higher regional risk baseline.
insights.quote: clearly intended for demonstration of force against Japan
insights.locator: In practice, China-Russia military coordination in Asia has expanded

insights.claim: China-Russia joint strategic bomber flights have escalated on a clear ladder: conducted annually since 2019, increased to twice a year since 2022, mutual landings in 2022, fighter escort flights in 2023, and the first confirmed participation of China's nuclear-capable H-6N bomber in 2024.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A documented year-by-year escalation ladder gives a template for forecasting the next increment of Sino-Russian military integration.
insights.locator: The Japanese government has paid particular attention to joint flights

insights.claim: The December 2025 China-Russia joint strategic bomber flight — the tenth — was timed to China's own political interests rather than shared Sino-Russian interests, indicating China can now apply pressure on Japan with the support of Russian military power at a moment of its own choosing.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The most consequential finding: Russia is now available as an on-demand pressure multiplier for Chinese coercion, which raises the intensity of any future Taiwan-related standoff.
insights.quote: China and Russia now have a relationship in which China can apply pressure on Japan with the support of Russian military power at a time that serves China’s political interests
insights.locator: Timing Aligned with China’s Political Interests

insights.claim: The trigger was Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's November 2025 Diet statement that Japan could recognize a 'survival-threatening situation' — the legal threshold for limited collective self-defense — if an armed attack on Taiwan and a maritime blockade developed to involve U.S. military intervention and attacks on U.S. vessels; the statement changed no Japanese law or policy yet China responded with diplomatic, economic and military pressure.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Chinese economic and military retaliation can be triggered by Japanese rhetorical positioning alone — a live tail risk for Japan-exposed trade and tourism sectors.
insights.locator: Timing Aligned with China’s Political Interests

insights.claim: The military pressure sequence ran from December 5, 2025, when multiple Chinese naval vessels including the aircraft carrier Liaoning transited the Southwest Islands into the Pacific, through December 6 when Liaoning-launched fighters directed radar at Japan Air Self-Defense Force aircraft twice with lock-on continuing intermittently for roughly 30 minutes, to the joint bomber flight on December 9.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A 30-minute radar lock-on is a near-miss incident class that could trigger an armed clash — evidence of how thin the accident margin has become.
insights.quote: In the second incident, radar lock-on continued intermittently for approximately 30 minutes.
insights.locator: On the military side, beginning on December 5, 2025

insights.claim: In the December 2025 flight two Russian Tu-95 bombers and two Chinese H-6 bombers joined over the East China Sea, passed through the Southwest Islands, then flew more than 600 miles in a straight line toward the Pacific off Shikoku on a trajectory that, if extended, would point toward the Tokyo area.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Route geometry is the escalation signal to watch — previous flights stayed near the Southwest Islands, so a Tokyo-pointing vector is a deliberate step up in coercive messaging.
insights.quote: flew more than 600 miles in a straight line toward the Pacific Ocean off Shikoku
insights.locator: A More Coercive Flight Route

insights.claim: The earlier politically timed precedent — the May 24, 2022 joint flight during the Quad summit in Tokyo — served shared China-Russia interests in countering U.S.-led regional coordination, whereas the December 2025 flight served China's Taiwan agenda specifically.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The shift from joint-interest to China-interest timing shows the relationship becoming asymmetric in China's favor — a structural change in how the pairing operates.
insights.locator: There is also an earlier example of a politically timed

insights.claim: Short-of-war pressure on Japan is intensifying on three axes simultaneously: horizontally, from China alone to China-Russia coordination; vertically, from conventional to nuclear-capable platforms; and qualitatively, with the behavior pattern itself becoming more coercive.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A three-axis escalation model usable for tracking gray-zone pressure in any theatre, including Taiwan and the South China Sea.
insights.locator: Assessment

insights.claim: While China escalated diplomatic, economic and military pressure on Japan, U.S. government agencies were relatively restrained in diplomatic messaging and public communication in support of Japan even as the alliance's military response was swift, visible and strong.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A gap between U.S. political and military signaling is a reliability question allies will price into their own hedging and defense buildouts.
insights.locator: The Nature of the U.S.-Japan Response

insights.claim: The first alliance response came on December 10, 2025 with a bilateral exercise over the Sea of Japan involving two U.S. B-52 strategic bombers, three JASDF F-35 fighters and three JASDF F-15 fighters, framed by Japan's Joint Staff as reaffirming a strong will not to tolerate unilateral changes to the status quo by force.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Establishes the baseline scale of alliance signaling against which subsequent escalation can be measured.
insights.quote: this bilateral exercise reaffirms the strong will between Japan and U.S. not to tolerate unilateral changes to the status quo by force
insights.locator: First Major Response

insights.claim: The first U.S.-Japan response did not stop the activity: on December 29, 2025 two Chinese H-6 bombers flew near the Southwest Islands with two intelligence-gathering aircraft and four fighters, and on January 21, 2026 two Russian Tu-95 bombers with two fighters repeatedly flew toward Japan over the Sea of Japan.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that a single show-of-force exercise does not reset adversary behavior — implying an escalating signaling requirement over time.
insights.locator: Continued Pressure

insights.claim: The second alliance response on February 16 and 18, 2026 involved four U.S. B-52 strategic bombers, six JASDF F-2 fighters and five JASDF F-15 fighters over the Sea of Japan and East China Sea — nearly double the aircraft of the first exercise, and the author could identify no publicly announced Japan-U.S. exercise from FY2020 to FY2025 with three or more B-52 bombers participating.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Four B-52s is an unprecedented signaling scale in six years of Japan-U.S. exercises — a concrete measure of how far alliance escalation has already moved.
insights.quote: The participation of four B-52s was therefore unusual in scale.
insights.locator: Second Major Response

insights.claim: After the second U.S.-Japan response, no similar China-Russia strategic bomber flights were conducted in the following weeks based on publicly available information, though Chinese and Russian intelligence-gathering aircraft including Y-9 and IL-20 continued operating around Japan.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Tentative evidence that scaled-up allied signaling can suppress the most provocative activity while lower-level pressure persists — the payoff calculus for escalated deterrence.
insights.locator: After the Second Response

insights.claim: Military coercion divides into deterrence, which prevents an unwanted action, and compellence, which induces a specific action such as stopping an ongoing action or reversing a change to the status quo — and whether a given response counts as one or the other depends on whether adversary activity is treated as discrete incidents or a continuing pattern.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A framing tool: the same military signal reads as defensive or coercive depending on the timeframe, which is exactly how escalation misreadings happen.
insights.locator: Assessment and Implications

insights.claim: In an environment of sustained and intensifying short-of-war pressure, the boundary between deterrence aimed at preventing further action and compellence aimed at stopping an ongoing pattern becomes blurred, so response frameworks built only around preventing armed attack or crisis onset are insufficient.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The alliance's own responses may be read by Beijing and Moscow as coercive rather than defensive, raising unintended escalation risk in the gray zone.
insights.locator: This suggests that, in an environment where increasingly intense

insights.claim: Even successful deterrence of further short-of-war actions can leave accumulated pressure or an unfavorable situation normalized as a fait accompli, meaning simply deterring further action could amount to accepting a deteriorated operational environment as a given.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Successful deterrence headlines can mask permanent erosion of the operating environment — the mechanism by which salami-slicing wins without a crisis.
insights.quote: Simply deterring further action could result in accepting a deteriorated operational environment as a given.
insights.locator: This framework does not suggest that Japan and the United States

themes.theme: Eight response approaches and alliance planning gaps

insights.claim: The author identifies at least eight response approaches to repeated short-of-war pressure: three deterrence-oriented (deter armed attack, deter crisis onset, deter further short-of-war actions) and five compellence-oriented, split into halt-type (stop a continuing series, stop an ongoing action), rollback-type (restore a situation created by a series of actions, or by a single action), and action-inducing-type (demand a new desired action).
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A concrete taxonomy for reading future U.S.-Japan moves; the appearance of rollback-type options in alliance planning would mark a significant policy escalation.
insights.locator: Policy Recommendations: Identifying and Examining Potential Alliance Response Approaches

insights.claim: Existing bilateral Flexible Deterrent Options are preplanned packages of diplomatic, informational, military and economic measures with both escalatory and de-escalatory effects, designed mainly to deter adversary actions before or during a crisis — which leaves them gapped against pressure that accumulates outside a crisis.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific doctrinal gap in existing alliance planning tools — the space where new joint planning and capability requirements will emerge.
insights.locator: In addition, through alliance coordination mechanisms

insights.claim: Japan and the United States should develop a shared threat perception that China-Russia coordination is already raising short-of-war pressure, reaffirm that responding to accumulated pressure is a common alliance interest, and comprehensively examine response approaches spanning deterrence through halt-, rollback- and action-inducing compellence.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The recommended agenda for the next round of U.S.-Japan strategic dialogue — a preview of what the accelerated 2026 strategy review may adopt.
insights.locator: As China-Russia coordination advances

insights.claim: Response options differ not only in timing, purpose and demand but in risk and required capabilities, so the allies must distinguish desirable from feasible options and, where a needed approach is not feasible, identify the constraints and jointly build alternatives to avoid response gaps.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Frames capability shortfalls as the binding constraint on alliance response — the specific driver of new capability procurement requests.
insights.locator: These response options differ not only in timing

insights.claim: Japan's Ministry of Defense has identified enhancing the effectiveness of the U.S.-Japan alliance from a strategic perspective as an issue requiring further consideration alongside strengthening deterrence and response capabilities in light of China-Russia and Russia-North Korea strategic coordination, and a strategic dialogue on alliance revitalization is once again taking shape.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Official Japanese institutional momentum toward an alliance-revitalization process — the political channel through which higher defense spending gets authorized.
insights.locator: Conclusion

insights.claim: China-Russia military coordination in Asia is no longer an abstract risk for a future contingency but has already emerged as operational pressure around Japan, and the U.S.-Japan alliance has begun to adapt to that environment.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The report's core reframing: treat Sino-Russian coordination as a present operational condition to be budgeted against, not a scenario to plan for.
insights.quote: China-Russia military coordination in Asia is no longer an abstract risk for a future contingency.
insights.locator: Conclusion
